spans.s:
Śiti-kakṣī in the taittirīya Saṃhitā is explained by Sāyaṇa as a ‘white-breasted’ (pāṇḍarodara) vulture. The word may, however, well be only an adjective.^2
Foot notes v. 5, 20, 1. Cf. Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 4; Av. v. 23, 5. Cf. Zimmer, Altindisches Leben, 93.

Śiti-pṛṣṭha (‘white-backed’) is the name of the Maitrāvaruṇa priest at the snake festival in the pañcaviṃśa brāhmaṇa.
Foot notes xxv. 15, 3. Cf. Weber, Indische Studien, 1, 35.

Śiti-bāhu aiṣakṛta Naimiśi is mentioned as a sacrificer in the Jaiminīya brāhmaṇa, where it is recorded that a monkey an off with his sacrificial cake.
Foot notes i. 363 (Journal of the American Oriental Society, 26, 192).

Śitpuṭa in the taittirīya Saṃhitā denotes, according to the commentator, a kind of cat.
Foot notes v. 5, 17, 1. Cf. Zimmer, Altindisches Leben, 86.

Sītā, ‘furrow,’ occurs in the Rigveda, and often later.
Foot notes iv. 57, 6. 7 (the most agricultural of Rigvedic hymns, and probably late).
Av. xi. 3, 12; taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 2, 5, 4. 5; 6, 2, 5; kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xx. 3, etc.
Cf. Hopkins, Journal of the American Oriental Society, 17, 86, n.
